title: Streets of Calcutta
tagline: A nun leaves the convent walls to serve the dying in the gutters of Calcutta.

scenes.text: Calcutta, 1948. A slight Albanian nun steps off a train and into the most overwhelming poverty on earth. She has left her comfortable teaching post at Loreto Convent — with permission from the Vatican, but without any money, any plan, or any helpers.

scenes.speaker: Mother Teresa
scenes.text: I heard a call within a call. It was a command to go to the poor and live among them. How can I teach clean, well-fed children about the love of God while the dying lie outside our gates?

challenge.question: In what year did Mother Teresa found the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta?
challenge.fact: Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity on 7 October 1950. Beginning with just 13 members in Calcutta, the congregation grew to over 4,500 sisters operating in 133 countries by the time of her death in 1997.

scenes.text: Teresa begins by washing the wounds of the sick on the streets of Motijhil, a slum behind Loreto Convent. She has no medicine, no building, no salary — only the certainty that each person is Christ in distressing disguise.

scenes.speaker: Mother Teresa
scenes.text: The biggest disease today is not leprosy or tuberculosis — it is the feeling of being unwanted, uncared for, and deserted by everybody. The greatest evil is the lack of love and charity.

challenge.instruction: With no building and no money, Teresa gathers the children of Motijhil in the open and teaches them in the dirt. Work out each sum and share out the bananas — a lesson and a meal together.
challenge.fact: When Mother Teresa left Loreto in 1948, she first took a short course in nursing with the Medical Mission Sisters in Patna, then came back to Calcutta to teach the children of Motijhil and visit the sick in their homes.

scenes.text: In 1950 she founds the Missionaries of Charity. In 1952 she opens Nirmal Hriday — Pure Heart — a home where the dying can be received from the streets and given a peaceful, dignified death, loved by someone.

scenes.speaker: Mother Teresa
scenes.text: We ourselves feel that what we are doing is just a drop in the ocean. But the ocean would be less because of that missing drop.

challenge.instruction: Nirmal Hriday is open, and the dying are brought in from the streets day and night. Draw up the sisters' rota so every duty is covered and no one is left alone.
challenge.fact: Each step built on the last: leaving the convent (1948) gave her freedom to serve; the Missionaries (1950) gave her sisters; Nirmal Hriday (1952) gave the dying dignity; and the Nobel Prize (1979) gave her voice to the world.

scenes.text: By the 1970s her work has spread to five continents. Governments give her free transport. The Pope grants buildings. In 1979 she flies to Oslo to collect the Nobel Peace Prize — and asks that the banquet money feed the poor instead.

scenes.speaker: Mother Teresa
scenes.text: Let us not be satisfied with just giving money. Money is not enough — money can be got. They need your hearts to love them. So spread your love everywhere you go.

challenge.instruction: News of the Nobel Prize reaches Calcutta by telex. Read the lamps to learn in whose name Teresa accepts it.
challenge.fact: By her death in 1997 the Missionaries of Charity had grown from a handful of sisters in Calcutta to more than 4,000, running some 610 missions in 123 countries — hospices, orphanages, and homes for people with leprosy and HIV/AIDS.

scenes.text: She dies in 1997 with little to her name. The Missionaries of Charity continue in 133 countries. In 2016 she is canonised — Saint Teresa of Calcutta — patron of the poor and the unwanted.

scenes.speaker: Mother Teresa
